plugin.hmac.title: HMAC (keyed-hash message authentication code)
plugin.hmac.preset.rfc4231-tc5-trunc: RFC 4231 test case 5: tag truncated to 128 bits
plugin.hmac.preset.rfc4231-tc6-longkey: RFC 4231 test case 6: 131-byte key, hashed first
plugin.hmac.preset.verify-fail: Verify a tag whose last byte is wrong (FAIL)
plugin.hmac.param.hashHint: The hash H inside HMAC. Its block size B sets the size of K0 and of the pads.
plugin.hmac.param.keyHint: 0 to 256 bytes as hex digits. A key longer than B is hashed first. Do not use a real key here.
plugin.hmac.param.encodingHint: Read the message as UTF-8 text or as hex bytes.
plugin.hmac.param.tagLengthHint: Keep the whole hash output or only its first bytes. At least half of the output and at least 10 bytes (RFC 2104 §5).
plugin.hmac.param.expectedHint: A tag to check against the computed one. Leave it empty to only compute.
plugin.hmac.op.innerBlock: Hash the block K0 ⊕ ipad (inner midstate)
plugin.hmac.op.outerBlock: Hash the block K0 ⊕ opad (outer midstate)
plugin.hmac.derivation.title: HMAC
plugin.hmac.formula.ipad: K0 ⊕ ipad, byte by byte: ipad = 36 in every byte
plugin.hmac.formula.opad: K0 ⊕ opad with opad = 5c; (K0 ⊕ ipad) ⊕ (K0 ⊕ opad) = 36 ⊕ 5c = 6a: the pads differ in 4 of 8 bits
plugin.hmac.step.initial: HMAC-{{hash}} authenticates a {{messageLength}}-byte message m with a {{keyLength}}-byte key K: tag = H((K0 ⊕ opad) ‖ H((K0 ⊕ ipad) ‖ m)), {{tagLength}} bytes. {{hash}} works on blocks of B = {{blockSize}} bytes and outputs L = {{outputLength}} bytes. This lab is a teaching tool: never type a real key into it.
plugin.hmac.step.keyPrep.exact: K0: the key has exactly B = {{blockSize}} bytes, so K0 = K.
plugin.hmac.step.keyPrep.padded: K0: the {{keyLength}}-byte key is shorter than a block (B = {{blockSize}} bytes), so zero bytes fill it up to B ({{zeros}} × 00): K0 = K ‖ 00…00.
plugin.hmac.step.keyPrep.hashed: K0: the {{keyLength}}-byte key is longer than a block (B = {{blockSize}} bytes), so it is hashed first (RFC 2104 §2): {{hash}}(K) = {{digest}}. Zero bytes then fill K0 up to B ({{zeros}} × 00). A key longer than B is therefore no stronger than the hash output.
plugin.hmac.step.ipad: K0 ⊕ ipad: each of the {{blockSize}} bytes of K0 is XORed with ipad = {{pad}} (byte 0: {{first}} ⊕ {{pad}} = {{result}}). The result fills exactly one block: the first block of the inner hash.
plugin.hmac.step.innerBlock.midstate: {{hash}} processes the block K0 ⊕ ipad. Its state afterwards is the inner midstate ({{stateLength}} bytes). It depends only on the key, so an implementation computes it once per key and reuses it for every message.
plugin.hmac.step.innerBlock.noMidstate: {{hash}} processes the block K0 ⊕ ipad. Its state afterwards depends only on the key, so an implementation can keep it per key. {{hash}} does not show this state here, so the lab has no midstate for it.
plugin.hmac.step.innerMessage: The inner hash continues with the {{messageLength}}-byte message: H((K0 ⊕ ipad) ‖ m) = {{inner}}. When the hash lab can take this input, the derivation view links to it.
plugin.hmac.step.opad: K0 ⊕ opad: the same with opad = {{pad}} (byte 0: {{first}} ⊕ {{pad}} = {{result}}). Because ipad ≠ opad, the inner and the outer hash start from different keys. Bellare, Canetti and Krawczyk (1996, §5.2) chose 36 and 5c for a simple representation and a high Hamming distance: 4 of 8 bits per byte.
plugin.hmac.step.outerBlock.midstate: {{hash}} processes the block K0 ⊕ opad: the outer midstate ({{stateLength}} bytes), again a pure function of the key. With both midstates stored, each further message costs only its own blocks plus the short outer hash.
plugin.hmac.step.outerBlock.noMidstate: {{hash}} processes the block K0 ⊕ opad. This outer state also depends only on the key and can be kept per key; {{hash}} does not show it here.
plugin.hmac.step.outer: The outer hash takes the {{outputLength}}-byte inner hash after K0 ⊕ opad: H((K0 ⊕ opad) ‖ inner hash) = {{digest}}. Because the outer hash wraps the inner one, nobody can append data to m and extend the tag, which H(K ‖ m) allows (length extension).
plugin.hmac.step.truncate: Truncation: the tag is the first {{tagLength}} of the L = {{outputLength}} bytes: {{tag}}. RFC 2104 §5 asks for at least half of L and at least 80 bits, here at least {{min}} bytes: a shorter tag is easier to guess.
plugin.hmac.step.verify.pass: Verify: for each of the {{expectedLength}} expected bytes, the lab XORs it with the tag byte at the same position and ORs the result into an accumulator. The loop never stops early, so the time does not reveal where a difference is. Accumulator = {{accumulator}}: the tags are equal, PASS.
plugin.hmac.step.verify.fail: Verify: each of the {{expectedLength}} expected bytes is XORed with the tag byte at the same position and ORed into an accumulator. Positions that differ: {{differences}}; accumulator = {{accumulator}}: FAIL. The loop still visited every byte: stopping at the first difference would let an attacker measure how many leading bytes of a forged tag are right.
plugin.hmac.step.verify.lengthMismatch: Verify: the expected tag has {{expectedLength}} bytes, the computed one {{tagLength}}. The loop still walks over all expected bytes before it reports FAIL, so its work does not depend on the content.
plugin.hmac.error.invalidParams: Give the hash, the key, the message, the tag length and the expected tag as text.
plugin.hmac.error.hash: Pick a hash function from the list.
plugin.hmac.error.keyLength: The key has {{length}} bytes; at most 256 are allowed.
plugin.hmac.error.inputLength: The message has {{length}} bytes; at most 256 are allowed.
plugin.hmac.error.expectedLength: The expected tag has {{length}} bytes; at most 64 are allowed.
plugin.hmac.error.tagLength: A {{length}}-byte tag does not fit {{hash}}: it needs {{min}} to {{max}} bytes (at least half of the hash output and at least 10 bytes, RFC 2104 §5).
